items.body_md:
On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here. Given the live motions practice in this case, the most plausible target is Google's August 21 Administrative Motion to Consider Whether Cases Should Be Related (Dkt. 478), whose response deadline was set at August 25 — the same date Dkt. 483 was filed. If that is the motion being opposed, the filing reflects a party — most likely the plaintiff class — resisting Google's effort to link this proceeding to one or more related cases. The case-relation motion, if granted, could shift judicial assignment or coordinate discovery and briefing schedules in ways that affect litigation pace and cost for both sides; if denied, each proceeding continues on its own track. Until Dkt. 483's full text is pulled from PACER, the identity of the filing party, the motion it targets, and the arguments advanced remain unverified and are not stated here.

The more consequential open question from yesterday remains unresolved in any available source: the outcome of the Dkt. 482 omnibus order — which adjudicates class certification, Google's sanctions motion, the outstanding intervention motion (Dkt. 468, Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix), and three motions for miscellaneous relief — has not been reported by any secondary outlet as of this briefing. The full text of Dkt. 482 on PACER is the controlling document. Until it is pulled, the class's shape, the sanctions disposition, and whether the intervenors were admitted remain unverified. The practical consequence is significant: class certification in this case defines the universe of copyright holders who can share in any statutory-damages recovery, and the per-work structure of § 504(c) means that the breadth of the certified class — authors only, publishers included, works defined by training vs. ingestion — directly sets the ceiling on Google's aggregate exposure.

The next concrete milestone is the resolution of the Dkt. 478 case-relation motion, which is now fully briefed with Dkt. 483's opposition and ripe for ruling. No hearing date is visible in the docket text for that motion. On the merits track, the full text of Dkt. 482 — available on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 — remains the priority pull; it is the document that determines where this case goes from here.

items.body_md:
On August 24, Judge Eumi K. Lee issued a cluster of orders in *In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation*, 5:23-cv-03440, resolving every major pending motion from the February 20 class certification hearing in a single day's docket activity. The central order is Dkt. 482 — an omnibus ruling that adjudicates the motion to certify the plaintiff class, Google's motion for sanctions, three motions for miscellaneous relief, an administrative motion under Civil Local Rule 7-11, and the outstanding motion to intervene. In a separate order (Dkt. 481), Judge Lee denied Dkt. 328, the Motion for Relief. Dkt. 480 granted Dkt. 269, Google's motion for leave to file supplemental authority — a routine procedural authorization that takes no classification above procedural-and-routine. Dkt. 479 resolved a sealing administrative motion, also procedural.

The operative question for recovery posture is the disposition in Dkt. 482 of the class certification motion. The docket entry confirms the order exists and that it resolves the certification motion, but does not recite the ruling's outcome in its text as reproduced here. What is confirmed: 
Judge Lee did not rule from the bench at the February 20 hearing on any of the motions to certify class, for sanctions, relief, or to intervene
 — meaning all four tracks were held under submission until this omnibus order. The sanctions motion is the one Google filed in November 2025, in which 
Google argued that plaintiffs had tried to "smuggle" in new classes into the lawsuit by seeking to certify multiple classes and subclasses of works "downloaded and/or ingested to develop" Google's generative AI models, whether used for training or not.
 Whether Judge Lee granted or denied sanctions — and whether she certified any class, a narrowed class, or none — are facts determinable only from the face of Dkt. 482 itself, which has not yet been reproduced in any secondary source confirmed in this cycle. The docket record is authoritative; the disposition is unverified and therefore not stated here.

What the chronology does establish is that this day's output concludes a phase of the case that has been under submission since February 20, approximately six months. The motion to certify class is substantive and dispositive of the plaintiff class's universe — certification defines who can share in any recovery and anchors the damages exposure Google faces on a per-work statutory-damages theory. 
Google's sanctions theory — that plaintiffs repositioned the case away from AI training by proposing classes defined around works "downloaded and/or ingested," not just trained-on — was briefed through February 5, 2026, with the hearing held February 20.
 Denial of the sanctions motion keeps plaintiffs' proposed class structure in play; a grant would have disciplinary and potentially structural consequences for class scope. The parallel denial of Dkt. 328 (Motion for Relief) closes a discrete contested track whose precise subject matter is not further described in the available docket text. On the intervention axis, Dkt. 482 also resolves the separate motion to intervene that remained pending after Cengage and Hachette withdrew their own intervention bid (Dkt. 342, resolved by Dkt. 477 on August 21) — the Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix motion filed at Dkt. 468 by consolidated plaintiffs, which had a hearing date set for February 20. The full text of Dkt. 482 — available on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 — is the next document to pull; it will determine the class's shape, the sanctions outcome, and the case trajectory from here.

items.body_md:
On August 21, Judge Eumi K. Lee entered an order — Dkt. 477 — resolving both an administrative motion and the pending motion to intervene filed by Cengage Learning and Hachette Book Group (Dkt. 342), formally closing the publisher-intervention track in *In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation*, 5:23-cv-03440. The companion administrative motion, Dkt. 478, filed the same day under Civil Local Rule 7-11, relates to that same intervention cluster. The order follows Cengage and Hachette's July 10 administrative motion to withdraw their intervention bid (Dkt. 473), which itself was contested — Google opposed it on July 14 (Dkt. 474) and the publishers sought leave to reply on July 15 (Dkt. 475). The August 21 order resolves that contested withdrawal proceeding.

The procedural endgame here tracks a strategic pivot that matters for recovery posture. 
With the new lawsuit, Cengage and Hachette withdrew their motion to take part in the 2023 suit, observing that Google could assert that a three-year statute of limitations pertains to the class member claims.
 That limitations concern, combined with the pendency of class certification in this case without a ruling on the intervention, drove the publishers to file a standalone action rather than remain tethered to a class whose scope and adequacy of representation they could not control. 
On July 13, 2026, Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning, Elsevier, and author Scott Turow filed a putative class action lawsuit against Google for willful infringement of millions of textual works to develop Google's Gemini large language models.
 
The proposed class action, filed July 10 in federal court in New York, accuses Google of illegally copying millions of works to train Gemini, including works scraped from "behind paywalls," from "known pirate sources," and books scanned and submitted via Google Books, Google Play, and Google Scholar.
 
The AAP stated the decision to file its own suit "aims to preserve the right to pursue all the claims that publishers and their authors have against Google, including important ones that fall outside the putative class in that case."


For claimants in the 5:23-cv-03440 class, the departure of Cengage and Hachette as proposed intervenors removes a potential source of publisher-side representation in the class certification calculus and eliminates the intra-class tension Google had been exploiting. 
Despite holding a hearing nearly five months ago on class certification, Judge Lee has yet to rule on the publishers' motion to intervene in the case
 — a delay that contributed to the publishers' decision to exit. The outstanding class certification ruling now becomes the next substantive milestone in this proceeding: that order will define the plaintiff class's composition and, directly, the universe of claimants able to share in any eventual recovery. No hearing date for the class certification ruling has been separately docketed; the next concrete date to watch is whenever Judge Lee issues that order.

items.lede: On August 13, the docket recorded a Notice of Appearance/Substitution/Change/Withdrawal of Attorney — procedural and routine, with no bearing on claim exposure or case trajectory.
items.body_md:
On August 13, the docket recorded a Notice of Appearance/Substitution/Change/Withdrawal of Attorney — procedural and routine, with no bearing on claim exposure or case trajectory.

The substantive posture entering today remains fixed on the unresolved motion sequence in the consolidated N.D. California action (5:23-cv-03440, Judge Lee). The most recent contested activity was the July 10–15 Cengage/Hachette motion to withdraw their intervention (Dkt. 473), Google's opposition (Dkt. 474), and the movants' administrative motion for leave to reply (Dkt. 475, with responses due July 20). That withdrawal, if granted, would remove the publisher intervenors from the consolidated track — a notable posture shift given that those same parties filed a separate, stand-alone action in the Southern District of New York on July 10 (
*Hachette Book Group et al. v. Google LLC*, No. 1:26-cv-05870, S.D.N.Y., with the complaint docketed July 10
). The two-track strategy — exit the intervention, press a direct action — concentrates the publishers' claims in a forum and on pleadings they fully control, rather than subordinating them to the consolidated class posture in California.

The New York complaint's theory is not procedurally identical to what was pending in the consolidated action. 
Hachette, Elsevier, Cengage, and Scott Turow allege Google used millions of copyrighted books and journal articles without permission to build Gemini, copying works from sources including Google Books, online libraries, and allegedly pirated websites
. 
The complaint separately alleges Google intentionally removed or changed copyright information to "conceal… that its Gemini Models were trained on stolen materials,"
 adding a DMCA § 1202 CMI-removal layer on top of the core infringement theory. 
The suit also argues Gemini now competes directly with the books it learned from by generating content that could reduce demand for the original materials
 — the § 107(4) market-harm prong that will be the decisive fair-use battleground across the AI-copyright track. The next concrete milestone in the N.D. California action is the outcome of the Dkt. 473/474/475 withdrawal motion sequence; once Judge Lee rules, the intervention question is resolved and the class certification record (indexed at Dkt. 472) governs the remaining plaintiff structure in the consolidated case.
